primary_sources: Paraphrase of the Atlantic Charter, August 1941
Paraphrase of the Declaration on Liberated Europe, Yalta, February 1945
Paraphrase of the Potsdam Protocol's decisions on Germany, August 1945
Paraphrase of the United Nations Charter, signed June 26, 1945
Description of the photograph of the Allied leaders at Potsdam, 1945

source: original; documents drawn from paraphrases of 1941-1945 conference declarations and charters, a table of the occupation zones, and a description of a 1945 photograph
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the wartime conferences of 1943-1945 laid the foundations for the Cold War.

documents.title: The Atlantic Charter
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Atlantic Charter, the joint statement by President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill, August 1941.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The two leaders said neither nation sought new territory, all peoples had the right to choose their own form of government, trade should be open, and all nations should be free from fear and want. They called for disarming aggressor nations and building a wider system of general security after the war.
documents.sourcing: A joint statement of war aims issued before the United States entered the war. It states hopes, not agreements with the Soviet Union.

documents.title: The Tehran Conference
documents.source: Paraphrase of the agreements reached at Tehran, Iran, November-December 1943, as described in Barron's Chapter 9.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin agreed that the invasion of France would go forward in 1944, timed with a major Soviet offensive. Stalin promised that the Soviet Union would join the war against Japan once Germany was defeated. The leaders agreed in principle to form a new international organization to keep the peace.
documents.sourcing: An account of a wartime meeting of the three leaders. It records military agreements, not a settlement of postwar Europe.

documents.title: The Declaration on Liberated Europe
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Declaration on Liberated Europe, agreed at Yalta, February 1945.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The three leaders declared that the peoples freed from German rule had the right to choose their own governments through free elections. The Allied governments promised to help those peoples form democratic governments and to hold free elections as soon as possible.
documents.sourcing: A promise made by all three leaders, including Stalin. Students should weigh the promise against what followed in Eastern Europe.

documents.title: Germany's occupation zones
documents.source: Table of the four occupation zones agreed at Yalta and confirmed at Potsdam, 1945.
documents.text:
| Zone | Occupying power |
| Southern Germany | United States |
| Northwestern Germany | Britain |
| Southwestern Germany | France |
| Eastern Germany | Soviet Union |

Berlin, inside the Soviet zone, was divided into four sectors.
documents.sourcing: A table of the agreed division. The zones were meant to be temporary, but they became the lines of the Cold War.

documents.title: The Potsdam decisions on Germany
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Potsdam Protocol's decisions on Germany, August 1945.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The leaders agreed to strip Germany of its military power, remove Nazis from public life, and rebuild German life on a democratic basis. Each occupying power would take reparations mainly from its own zone, and the Soviet Union would also receive part of the industrial equipment removed from the western zones.
documents.sourcing: A protocol agreed by the three powers after Germany's surrender. Its reparations rule let each power treat its own zone as it chose.

documents.title: The United Nations Charter
documents.source: Paraphrase of the purposes set out in the United Nations Charter, signed at San Francisco, June 26, 1945.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The Charter said the United Nations would keep the peace, settle disputes without war, and encourage cooperation among nations. In the Security Council, five permanent members, the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France, and China, could each block a decision by veto.
documents.sourcing: A founding document signed by 50 nations. It shows the Allies still building shared institutions even as they disagreed over Europe.

documents.title: The new leaders at Potsdam
documents.source: Description of the photograph of the Allied leaders at Potsdam, circa July 28 to August 1, 1945 (USA C-1860).
documents.text: Description: The photograph shows three men seated in wicker chairs outdoors: British Prime Minister Clement Attlee, President Harry S. Truman, and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. Four advisers stand behind them. Two of the seated men differ from the leaders photographed at Yalta five months earlier.
documents.sourcing: A photograph taken during the conference. It shows new faces, but the Soviet leader, Stalin, is the one face that did not change.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the wartime conferences of 1943-1945 laid the foundations for the Cold War, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the wartime alliance against Germany and Japan, the failure of the League of Nations, or the Soviet Union carrying most of the fighting against Germany before 1944.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or describing them without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Soviet installation of a Communist government in Poland, the division of Berlin, the atomic monopoly, or the Potsdam Declaration's demand for Japan's unconditional surrender.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to the Cold War with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation, such as a promise made by all three leaders that later failed, a protocol agreed after Germany's surrender, or a photograph that shows new faces but the same Soviet leader.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an author without explaining why the authorship matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing a complex understanding, such as explaining that the conferences both built shared institutions and left the disputes that split the alliance, or weighing cooperation against conflict across the documents.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument that treats the conferences as only cooperative or only divisive does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: the conferences laid the foundations for the Cold War to a large extent, because they settled how to win the war while leaving the shape of postwar Europe open, and the open questions were then settled by armies on the ground rather than by agreement.

Group 1, cooperation: Documents 1, 2, and 6, the Atlantic Charter, Tehran, and the United Nations Charter, show the Allies building shared aims and institutions. Group 2, promises that failed: Documents 3 and 4, the Declaration on Liberated Europe and the occupation zones, promised free elections and temporary zones, but Soviet-backed governments took power and the zones hardened into borders. Group 3, new tensions: Documents 5 and 7, the Potsdam reparations rule and the photograph of new leaders, show the powers drifting apart once Germany was gone.

Outside evidence: the Soviet installation of a Communist government in Poland, the division of Berlin, and the American atomic monopoly. Complexity: the same conferences that built the United Nations also drew the lines the Cold War followed, so cooperation and conflict came from the same meetings.
